title: Detection of Generate Content
summary: This detection strategy looks for content produced at machine scale by generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools, whether that is text, images, audio or video, in the service of deception. It covers technique T1683 and matters because generation removes the historical cost of writing believable lures, so one operator can now produce thousands of individually coherent messages, personas or voice clips. The telemetry that makes it possible is mail and collaboration content metadata, stylometric and language model enrichment scores, file metadata including content provenance records, and outbound requests to public AI service endpoints. In practice the strategy fails because legitimate staff use the same tools every day, generated text is designed to look human, and detection scores are probabilistic. Analysts therefore rely on volume, uniformity and timing rather than on a single score, and treat provenance metadata as corroboration instead of proof.

beginner.definition: Generative artificial intelligence is software that creates new text, pictures or sound. This detection looks for content made that way at large scale to trick people. It catches campaigns, not one single message.
beginner.whyItMatters: In the past, a bad message was often badly written. That is no longer true. A machine can write thousands of polite, correct messages in an hour. Each one can sound like a real person. Because the quality is high, people trust it more, so detection must look at the pattern across many messages.
howItWorks: You collect message metadata. This includes the sender, timing, length and the recipients.
You measure how similar the messages are. Machine output is often very uniform.
You check how quickly accounts or messages are created. Machines do not need sleep.
You read provenance data where it exists. It records how a file was made.
You watch for outbound requests to public artificial intelligence services from unusual hosts.
You group the signals into one campaign alert, with examples for the analyst to read.
beginner.example: Picture a handwriting competition. One entry looks beautiful, and nobody would question it. Then you notice two hundred entries, all in the same neat style, all delivered within ten minutes. The single page was never the problem. The pattern across all the pages is what tells you a machine wrote them.
takeaways: Generated content is hard to judge one item at a time, so look at the campaign.
Uniformity, volume and strange timing are stronger signals than writing style.
Content provenance records help, but they can be removed or forged.

objectives: Describe how generative artificial intelligence (AI) changes the economics of producing deceptive content
Identify the metadata fields that reveal machine scale production, such as timing clusters and near duplicate bodies
Interpret content provenance metadata and explain why its absence is weak evidence
Correlate generation activity with account creation, first contact messaging and credential requests
Choose between content scoring, volume thresholds and behavioural clustering for a given channel
Explain the privacy and accuracy limits of stylometric scoring on employee communications
dataSources: Mail gateway message metadata including send timestamps, message body hash, body length, subject line and recipient count
Collaboration platform audit events recording account creation, profile photo upload and bulk message or invitation sending
Content provenance metadata embedded in image, audio and video files recording the producing tool and generation history
Outbound web proxy logs showing requests to public generative artificial intelligence (AI) service endpoints with bytes uploaded
Endpoint process creation records showing browser or scripting interpreter sessions that submit large text uploads to external services
logic: The pattern is content that is individually plausible but statistically part of a machine produced batch. You correlate message timestamps, body hashes and lengths across a sending account or a group of accounts, and combine that with account age, profile completeness and first contact behaviour toward recipients. The malicious case is a burst of near identical bodies with small variable substitutions, sent from accounts created in the same short window, often to recipients who have no prior relationship with the sender, sometimes followed by a credential or payment request. The benign case is a legitimate marketing or notification platform sending templated mail from an established, authenticated domain with a long history and a clear business relationship. Account age and relationship history separate the two far more reliably than any text classifier score.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Bulk Near Duplicate Messages From Newly Created Accounts
# logsource:
#   product: windows
#   service: email
# detection:
#   selection:
#     account_age_days: < 7
#     recipient_count: > 25
#     body_similarity: > 0.9
#     first_contact: true
#   filter:
#     sender_domain: 'trusted-notifications.example'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: Marketing automation platforms sending a templated campaign from a newly provisioned but legitimate sending subdomain
Human resources systems delivering the same onboarding message to a large intake group on one day
Conference organisers sending near identical speaker invitations from a short lived event domain
Customer relationship management tools that generate personalised but structurally identical follow up mail
Employees using approved assistants to draft routine replies, producing similar phrasing across a team
tuningNotes: Allowlist established sending domains and automated platforms first, then tune the similarity threshold against a fortnight of real mail so that ordinary templates do not alert. Scope the rule to external inbound and newly created outbound accounts rather than all internal mail, and prefer grouping alerts by campaign so that one burst becomes one ticket instead of hundreds. Add content provenance checks only for file sharing and media channels, where they are meaningful. Excluding internal mail means you lose visibility of an insider using generation tools, so keep a lower severity rule on unusually high volume sending from individual internal mailboxes.
